content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli raab (also known as rapini or mustard greens) is a leafy cruciferous vegetable native to the Mediterranean and Asia. It has a mildly bitter, nutty flavor and a crisp texture. It is eaten raw in salads or lightly sautéed or braised.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli raab is rich in glucosinolates, which convert to beneficial sulforaphanes when the plant is cut.
In Italy it is called “rapini” and is a staple in traditional Piedmont cuisine.
Leaves, stems, and even the flower buds are edible.
Its vitamin K content exceeds that of regular broccoli.
Ancient Romans used it as a fragrant seasoning.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamins A and C
items.content: These vitamins aid vision, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides calcium and iron
items.content: These minerals contribute to strong bones and healthy blood formation.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health and helps with weight management.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to broccoli raab.

items.title: Glucosinolates content
items.content: In large amounts, glucosinolates can irritate the stomach of sensitive people.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Broccoli raab contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation when consumed excessively.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Leaves and stems can be eaten raw in salads, added to smoothies, or quickly sautéed in olive oil. Braised or roasted broccoli raab retains its crunch and flavor. Before cooking, rinse and trim thick stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store broccoli raab in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container, where it stays fresh for 3‑5 days. Do not wash before storing to avoid excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: The "Chocolate Wafer" cookie is a crisp wafer roll coated with a layer of milk chocolate. It is made from wheat flour, sugar, vegetable fats and cocoa butter, offering a sweet, slightly bitter flavor and a light texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wafer cookies first appeared in Europe in the 19th century as a light tea snack.
The chocolate coating usually covers only one side of the wafer, creating a contrast between crunchy texture and smooth glaze.
Caramelization of sugar in the dough gives the characteristic golden color.
The cookie is often sold in single‑serve packages, convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.
In some countries the "Chocolate Wafer" is a traditional holiday gift.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Contains fast‑acting carbohydrates that quickly raise blood glucose, providing immediate energy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa butter in the chocolate coating is rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Provides small amounts of iron that support normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies modest amounts of B1, B2 and niacin, involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Satiety satisfaction
items.content: Sweet taste and crunchy texture promote a feeling of fullness and may reduce overeating.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some versions are coated with vegetable fats containing trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain gluten, soy lecithin and milk chocolate—potential allergens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cookie is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, paired with coffee or tea, or incorporate it into desserts—crumble into ice cream, yogurt or baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in an airtight package. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated to prevent the chocolate coating from melting.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter and jelly is a classic sandwich made of creamy peanut butter and sweet fruit jelly, usually served between two slices of bread. The salty‑sweet combination makes it a favorite snack worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial peanut butter recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1900s.
Traditional American "PB&J" is often made with whole‑grain bread and grape or strawberry jam.
During World War II, peanut butter was a staple for soldiers as a source of protein and energy.
There are over 300 varieties of jam that can be paired with peanut butter, from classic strawberry to exotic mango and passion fruit.
In the 1970s the first "children's" peanut butter was introduced, fortified with vitamins and without added sugar.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 % protein, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in peanut butter is monounsaturated, which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanut butter contains niacin, thiamine, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in the jelly
items.content: Fruit jelly is rich in vitamins C and E and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of fats and carbohydrates provides a quick and sustained energy source.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Prepared jams often contain added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and tooth decay.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A PB&J sandwich is relatively high in calories; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Some peanut butter varieties are salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread an even layer of peanut butter on one slice of bread, top with jelly, and place the second slice on top. You can add banana, honey, or nuts for extra flavor. The sandwich is portable for on‑the‑go meals and can also be used as a filling for rolls and cupcakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store an opened jar of peanut butter in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation. Keep jelly in a cool, dry place; after opening, refrigerate and use within 1‑2 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: The whole grain white hamburger bun (item 2516) is made from whole wheat flour, with a modest amount of sugar, salt, and vegetable oil. It has a soft, slightly springy crumb and a light‑brown crust, making it an ideal base for any type of burger.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain buns retain more nutrients than refined‑flour equivalents.
The white crust is achieved with a small amount of sugar and milk, which promote caramelization.
Traditionally these buns are baked in a steam oven, giving them a tender interior.
In the United States they are a staple in fast‑food chains, but are also popular for home‑made burgers.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white buns, whole‑grain varieties raise blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and zinc are present, contributing to immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and a modest amount of protein help you feel full longer.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten intolerance should avoid this bun.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although moderate, those monitoring sodium intake should account for it in their diet.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The bun contains carbohydrates and some fat, so portion size should be considered when managing weight.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the bun as the base for classic hamburgers, build sliders, make mini‑burgers, or serve it alongside soups. Lightly toasting it adds a pleasant crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep buns in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Warm in the oven or toaster before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey tail (Trametes versicolor) is a mushroom that grows on dead wood in temperate regions. Its colorful, banded caps resemble a turkey’s tail, giving the fungus its common name. It is used dried in soups and broths, and valued in traditional medicine for its potential immune‑modulating properties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the distinctive striped pattern on the cap.
It has been used in Asian traditional medicine for over 2,000 years.
Dried slices are often added to broths for flavor and color.
Rich in polysaccharides, especially beta‑glucans, it is a focus of scientific research.
In nature it helps decompose wood, recycling nutrients in forest ecosystems.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Turkey tail extracts contain beta‑glucans that may enhance the activity of immune cells.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: The mushroom is high in polyphenols that can neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Fiber in dried slices supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effects
items.content: Compounds in the fungus have been shown to reduce inflammatory markers in some studies.

items.title: Blood sugar balance
items.content: Preliminary research suggests modest reductions in glucose levels with regular consumption.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience mushroom‑related allergies.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improperly dried or stored specimens can develop harmful toxins.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Beta‑glucans may amplify the effects of immunosuppressive drugs; consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Not for children and pregnant women
items.content: Safety of high‑dose intake in these groups has not been established.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried turkey tail slices are typically steeped in hot water and simmered for 20‑30 minutes, then used as a flavoring in soups, broths, and sauces. They can also be ground into a powder for teas or smoothies. When taken as capsules or extracts, follow the manufacturer’s dosage guidelines.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry slices in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate them. Discard any product that shows mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.
